text: The blacksmith sells iron nails, horseshoes and a dented helm, and will not haggle before the forge is hot.
A travelling alchemist offers tinctures for fever and for sleep, priced by the phial and not the dram.
The tanner will trade cured hide for salt or for good rope, and swears the salt is worth more.
Fresh bread, two coppers a loaf, and the miller wants his due before the week turns again.
The fletcher has goose-feather arrows and one yew longbow left, kept behind the counter for a serious buyer.
A cooper mends barrels near the well and grumbles about the rain, which has swollen every stave.
The apothecary keeps dried nightshade behind the counter, locked, and asks who sent you first.
Wool from the north sells poorly this season, the weaver says, and she blames the roads.
The stabler charges three coppers a night and feeds the horse oats, or hay for two.
A scribe copies letters for a fee and reads them for another, and remembers every name.
The potter fired a kiln of bowls and cracked half of them, so the rest cost double.
Salted fish, barrels of it, hauled up from the river landing before the market bell rings.
The chandler makes tallow candles that smoke and beeswax that does not, and knows what you can afford.
A mason quarries stone for the new gatehouse and wants more hands, paid at week's end.
The herbalist gathers yarrow at dawn and sells it bundled by the dozen, roots still damp.
Ale is thin this year; the brewer blames the barley, and the drinkers blame the brewer.
